source.title: Multi-Modal Continual Learning via Cross-Modality Adapters and Representation Alignment with Knowledge Preservation
source.authors: Evelyn Chee; Wynne Hsu; Mong Li Lee

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies alignment among modality-specific and joint representations inside a single multimodal continual-learning model. It does not test convergence between independently trained models, convergence with scale or capability, or the other listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper compares representation-alignment training objectives and describes t-SNE representations. These results concern within-model multimodal alignment, not convergence across models as specified in the claim. Its other continual-learning accuracy and forgetting results do not measure the claim.
record.test_reason: A multimodal continual-learning method paper. It trains alignment losses inside one model and reports classification accuracy and forgetting. It never compares representations of independently trained models, seeds or modality-specific models. It does not cite either original source and does not use convergence as a tool. Its alignment is induced by its own loss, not measured as arising on its own.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that cross-modality mixture-of-experts adapters plus a relaxed alignment loss and a relation-preservation loss beat continual-learning baselines on AVE, UESTC-MMEA and SAMSEMO. They report higher accuracy and lower forgetting. The alignment-loss comparison is one ablation, not the headline result.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes and evaluates a multimodal continual-learning framework; it does not reproduce the original convergence methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper compares conventional multimodal supervised contrastive loss with its proposed Lalign objective and reports different classification outcomes and qualitative representation visualizations.

fits_no_version.finding: On AVE, aligning each modality to a fused joint representation beat direct multimodal supervised contrastive alignment. Accuracy was 91.91 versus 90.46, and t-SNE showed more distinct modality clusters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within a trained multimodal model, strict contrastive cross-modal alignment discards modality-specific information compared with a relaxed alignment objective.

record.problems: The representation comparisons are qualitative t-SNE visualizations and do not compare independently trained models or measure convergence across models. Numerical results shown here concern continual-learning performance rather than representational similarity.
record.rows_left_out: Table 5 loss-component ablations and the remaining continual-learning accuracy and forgetting results were left out because those outcomes do not measure representation convergence or its geometry. Other tables and figures on adapter performance and expert counts were likewise outside the claim.

untested.parts: All: no cross-model comparison across scale or capability.
All: no measure of vision-language alignment on paired data versus model quality.
All: no mapping, stitching or relative-representation tests between models.
All: no feature or circuit comparison across models.
All: no similarity-metric or input-distribution sensitivity of convergence.
All: no measure of convergence extent, plateau, or its causes.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is unrelated to the representation-convergence claim. It is better seen as a T6 study that merely uses the word 'alignment' for a training objective. All rows are own-method ablations with versions 'none'.

versions.untested_parts: No comparison of independently trained models across size or capability.
No test of paired image-caption representations from vision and language models, or of alignment rising with model performance.
No comparison of seeds, features or shared subspaces across same-architecture networks.
No test of mapping or stitching representations between models, or of unpaired mapping.
No comparison of recurring interpretable features or circuits across models.
The paper compares alignment objectives, but does not test convergence under alternative similarity measures, settings or input distributions.
No test of cross-model convergence plateaus or whether shared training data or objectives explain it.
